I'll share my limited research on this topic, but would love your (or your legal team's) perspective. To be clear, the concern I have is with what I'll call "PDF certificates". California Corporations Code § 416(a) provides (emphasis added): "Every holder of shares is entitled to a certificate signed in the name of the corporation by the chairperson or vice chairperson of the board or the president or a vice president and by the secretary or an assistant secretary, or the chief financial officer or an assistant treasurer, and may be sealed with the seal of the corporation, if any. The signatures on the certificates may be facsimile signatures." Nothing in § 416(a) authorizes replacing the certificate itself with an entirely digital file. The statute still presupposes a "certificate" as a tangible instrument — presumably, the physical evidence of a certificated security. In other words, this section merely allows the signatures to be facsimiles, but says nothing about the certificate itself. The only statutory exception to issuing a paper certificate is going to a full-on uncertificated system (section 416(b), quoted below). As far as I can tell, there is only one real counterargument: The federal E-SIGN general rules. E-SIGN seems to say that a record can't be denied legal effect solely because it is electronic. The problem, though, is Section 416(a) and (b) [which provides for non-certificated shares] don't say that. They simply say that a holder is entitled to a signed certificate. Also, not clear that E-SIGN covers property concepts like stock certificates. Also, Article 8 of the UCC defines certificated security as one represented by a certificate, and another section states that delivery requires "possession", which implies it is physical. So, E-SIGN is less than clear. So, without having dug into this too much, my sense is that to be clearly within the law, you need to use the non-certificated security approach in Section 416(b) [clearly allowed], rather than using images or PDFs of actual physical stock certificates [not clearly allowed as far as I can tell]. Perhaps this is a case where practice and the nuances of the statutory schedule don't fully line up yet. If payment ultimately cannot be collected, Carta would look to recover the funds that were passed to the company and assist you with reversing the exercise on the platform so the cap table accurately reflects the outcome. Proposed responses below: *Why are the TCs addressed to "you" instead of a company?* Carta's Terms of Service govern the general conduct of individual end-users (both administrators and security holders) who interact with the platform. The company-level relationship is governed by the Master Subscription Agreement (< which is the operative contract between Carta and your company. Section 14.6 of the MSA includes conflict language providing that the MSA overrides the Terms of Service to the extent of any conflict. *How many user licenses do we have, and do shareholders get licenses?* Carta's pricing is based on the number of Security Holders on your cap table, as reflected in your Order Form under the MSA. There is no limit on the number of administrative "Users" your company can authorize to manage the cap table. Both administrative users and security holders access the platform under different permissions, but the Terms of Service license provisions do not govern this. *Is stockholder data a "Submission" that Carta can treat as non-confidential?* No. Stockholder data submitted through the platform falls within the definition of "Customer Data" under the MSA, which covers data submitted to Hosted Services by the Customer, on its behalf by its Users (i.e., administrative users), and information submitted by Security Holders directly related to the Carta Services provided to the Customer. Customer Data protections in the MSA, not the Submissions provision in the Terms of Service, control here. Examples of "Submissions" that would _not_ constitute Customer Data include information an end user voluntarily provides through their Carta account related to discussion boards, surveys, questionnaires, promotions, or requests for product feedback. *Are we purchasing a license to Services under the Terms of Service?* The license to your company's Carta services is granted under the MSA and your Order Form, not under the "License to Services" section of the Terms of Service. That section of the Terms governs individual end-user access to Carta's general platform features. Your commercial license terms (scope, restrictions, term) are defined in the Order Form and MSA.
